name: Unripe olive oil hair removal

lead: Unripe olive oil hair removal is a folk method in which oil from olives picked well before ripeness was applied to the body to remove or discourage hair. It is mentioned in ancient Jewish legal discussion and sits within the long history of body-hair removal for a smoother look.
The practice is known mainly from historical texts rather than modern studies. No published trials have tested whether it removes hair.

paras: Historical sources describe the oil being used as a depilatory in some cultures; details of preparation are not well documented, and it is not a standard modern method.
No safety data exist for this use. Olive oil is a common skin product, and as with any topical, individual skin reactions are possible.

chain: Oil from unripe olives applied to skin
Believed to loosen or discourage body hair
angle.text: Historically, people used the oil as a depilatory so that body hair would be reduced for a smoother appearance. It is documented as an ancient practice rather than a tested one.

lead: Unripe olive oil hair removal refers to the use of oil pressed from olives that had not reached full ripeness as a depilatory, a way of getting a smooth, hairless skin surface. The Wikipedia article on hair removal notes that oil from olives under about one-third of their natural ripeness was used in some cultures for this purpose, citing the Babylonian Talmud (tractate Menahot 86a) [1].

It belongs to a broad history of depilation. Hair removal has been practiced in nearly all human cultures since at least the Neolithic era, with Egyptians using pumice and razors and Greeks and Romans using depilatory preparations and attendants [1].
No modern clinical studies of unripe olive oil as a hair remover are known.

paras: Accounts describe oil from olives pressed before ripening, used in some cultures to remove body hair [1]. Details such as preparation and frequency are not well documented in accessible sources.

Ancient depilatories included psilothrum and dropax in Greece and Rome, and an abrasive paste of slaked lime, ash and orpiment that is still used in parts of rural India and Iran [1]. Unripe olive oil is one of several plant-based approaches recorded.
